description: Practical data engineering on AWS, Azure and Kubernetes: cloud storage and table formats, stateful data on K8s, Kafka and managed streaming, warehousing/lakehouse, and data gravity and cost. For platform architects; storage-engine and consistency theory lives in the Distributed Systems & Data deck.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::01 Cloud Storage & Table Formats
notes.front: Block storage: traits, AWS/Azure services, Kubernetes access mode?
notes.back: Single-attach, low-latency disk with a filesystem on top. AWS Elastic Block Store (EBS) · Azure Managed Disk · persistent volume (PV) with ReadWriteOnce.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::01 Cloud Storage & Table Formats
notes.front: File storage: traits, AWS/Azure services, Kubernetes access mode?
notes.back: Shared network filesystem. AWS Elastic File System (EFS) / FSx · Azure Files / Azure NetApp Files · persistent volume (PV) with ReadWriteMany.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::01 Cloud Storage & Table Formats
notes.front: Object storage: traits, AWS/Azure services, and how Kubernetes pods reach it?
notes.back: HTTP API, flat namespace, immutable objects, cheapest and most durable. S3 · Azure Blob / Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) Gen2. No native persistent volume (PV): software development kit (SDK), or container storage interface (CSI) drivers like Mountpoint for S3 / BlobFuse.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::01 Cloud Storage & Table Formats
notes.front: What are Parquet and Optimized Row Columnar (ORC)?
notes.back: Columnar, self-describing file formats for analytics, with per-column encoding and compression (dictionary, run-length encoding (RLE), Snappy/ZSTD). Parquet dominates on AWS and Azure.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::01 Cloud Storage & Table Formats
notes.front: How do Parquet files let a query engine on S3/Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) skip data?
notes.back: Predicate pushdown: per-row-group min/max statistics skip whole chunks. Column pruning: byte-range GETs fetch only the requested columns.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::01 Cloud Storage & Table Formats
notes.front: What problem do open table formats (Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi) solve?
notes.back: Object storage gives you files, not tables. A metadata layer over Parquet adds atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability (ACID) multi-file commits and safe concurrent writers.
notes.analogy: A library catalogue over a pile of books: the books don't change, but the catalogue decides atomically which ones are 'on the shelf'.
notes.extra: AWS: Iceberg via Glue Catalog, Athena, S3 Tables. Azure: Delta is native to Fabric OneLake and Databricks.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::01 Cloud Storage & Table Formats
notes.text: Beyond atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability (ACID) commits, table formats give {{c1::time travel}} (query old snapshots), {{c2::schema evolution}}, hidden partitioning, and {{c3::row-level updates/deletes}} (needed for change data capture (CDC) and General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) erasure).

notes.deck: Data Engineering::01 Cloud Storage & Table Formats
notes.text: {{c1::Data lake}}: raw files in cheap object storage, schema-on-read. {{c2::Data warehouse}}: curated, schema-on-write, columnar engine with its own storage (Redshift, Snowflake). {{c3::Lakehouse}}: warehouse semantics on open table formats in the lake (Databricks, Fabric, Athena + Iceberg).

notes.deck: Data Engineering::02 Stateful Data on Kubernetes
notes.front: Why are Elastic Block Store (EBS) volumes and Azure Managed Disks a scheduling concern for stateful pods?
notes.back: They're zonal: a disk can attach only to nodes in its own availability zone (AZ), so a pod rescheduled to another zone can't mount its volume.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::02 Stateful Data on Kubernetes
notes.front: How do you keep a stateful pod and its zonal disk together?
notes.back: volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer (provision where the pod lands), topology-aware scheduling, and replication across zones in the application rather than the disk.
notes.extra: Azure also offers zone-redundant storage (ZRS) disks; AWS has no cross-availability-zone (AZ) Elastic Block Store (EBS).

notes.deck: Data Engineering::02 Stateful Data on Kubernetes
notes.front: Why run a database or Kafka broker as a StatefulSet, not a Deployment?
notes.back: Each replica gets a stable identity (ordinal name, DNS via headless Service) and its own persistent volume claim (PVC) that follows it; ordered rollouts protect quorum. Deployments treat pods as interchangeable.
notes.analogy: Deployments are hotel rooms (any free one will do); StatefulSets are named rented flats with your own furniture inside.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::02 Stateful Data on Kubernetes
notes.front: What do the cloud container storage interface (CSI) drivers (Elastic Block Store (EBS), Azure Disk) add beyond mounting a volume?
notes.back: Dynamic provisioning, online expansion, VolumeSnapshot and cloning, and topology reporting so the scheduler knows the volume's zone.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::02 Stateful Data on Kubernetes
notes.front: What are the two layers of backup for stateful workloads on Kubernetes?
notes.back: Volume level: container storage interface (CSI) VolumeSnapshots (Elastic Block Store (EBS)/Azure Disk snapshots), orchestrated with Velero. Application level: native backups to object storage (pgBackRest/WAL-G, MirrorMaker 2).

notes.deck: Data Engineering::02 Stateful Data on Kubernetes
notes.front: Why prefer application-level backups over disk snapshots for a running database?
notes.back: A disk snapshot of a live database is only crash-consistent; native tools give consistent, point-in-time-recoverable backups.
notes.extra: Cross-region restores of multi-TB data are bandwidth-bound: set recovery time objective (RTO) accordingly.

notes.text: Kafka: a {{c1::topic}} is a named append-only stream; it is split into {{c2::partitions}}, ordered immutable logs that are the unit of parallelism and replication; an {{c3::offset}} is a record's sequence number within one partition.
notes.analogy: A topic is a multi-lane motorway; each lane (partition) keeps its own order, and an offset is a milestone on one lane.

notes.front: What ordering guarantee does Kafka give?
notes.back: Ordering only within a partition. Events that must stay ordered (e.g. per customer) need the same key; global order needs one partition, which caps throughput.
notes.analogy: Like checkout lanes: each lane serves its own queue in order, but there's no ordering between lanes.

notes.front: How does a record's key pick its partition, and what goes wrong with a skewed key?
notes.back: Default: hash(key) mod partitions. One dominant key overloads one partition, so one broker and one consumer bottleneck while others idle.
notes.extra: Fixes: salt/sub-key, more partitions, or give up per-entity ordering.

notes.front: How do Kafka consumer groups divide work?
notes.back: Consumers sharing a group.id split the partitions: each partition goes to exactly one consumer in the group. Different groups each get the full stream.
notes.analogy: A team splitting a stack of mailbags: each bag goes to exactly one sorter, and another team gets its own copy of every bag.

notes.front: What limits a Kafka consumer group's parallelism?
notes.back: The partition count: consumers beyond it sit idle. Membership changes trigger a rebalance (cooperative rebalancing reduces the pause).

notes.front: Why choose a Kafka topic's partition count deliberately up front?
notes.back: Partitions can't be shrunk, and adding them changes hash(key) mod N, breaking per-key ordering for existing keys.

notes.front: What is Kafka's in-sync replica set (ISR)?
notes.back: The partition's followers that are fully caught up with the leader. Only ISR members can become leader without data loss.
notes.analogy: The understudies who have rehearsed every line so far: only they can step in for the lead without the audience noticing.

notes.text: Kafka durability: {{c1::replication.factor=3}} (three copies across availability zones (AZs)) + {{c2::acks=all}} (producer waits for the in-sync replica set (ISR)) + {{c3::min.insync.replicas=2}} (reject writes with fewer in sync) survives one broker/AZ loss without data loss.
Kafka consumer semantics: commit the offset {{c1::before}} processing → at-most-once (crash loses messages); commit {{c2::after}} processing → at-least-once (crash causes duplicates).
notes.analogy: Ticking a to-do item before doing it (may never happen) vs after doing it (may happen twice if you forget you did it).

notes.front: What does Kafka exactly-once need?
notes.back: Idempotent producer (enable.idempotence) + transactions (atomic writes to several partitions plus the offset commit) + isolation.level=read_committed consumers.

notes.front: Where does Kafka exactly-once stop applying?
notes.back: At the edge of Kafka: it holds for Kafka→Kafka pipelines (Kafka Streams). Writing to an external system needs idempotent sinks or two-phase commit (2PC).

notes.front: Kafka time/size retention vs log compaction?
notes.back: Retention (cleanup.policy=delete): drop old segments; for event streams. Compaction (compact): keep the latest record per key forever; for changelogs and state.
notes.analogy: Retention is a CCTV tape overwritten after 30 days; compaction is a contacts list that keeps only each person's latest number.
notes.extra: A null value is a tombstone that deletes the key. Both policies can be combined.

notes.front: What is Kafka consumer lag, and why is it the main health metric?
notes.back: Latest offset − committed offset: how far behind a consumer is. Growing lag means consumers can't keep up. Also the usual Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling (KEDA)/horizontal pod autoscaler (HPA) scaling signal.
notes.analogy: The gap between the conveyor belt and the worker: growing piles mean the worker can't keep up.
notes.extra: Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK): MaxOffsetLag; self-run: Burrow, kafka-exporter.

notes.front: ZooKeeper vs KRaft: what changed in Kafka's control plane?
notes.back: Metadata moved from an external ZooKeeper ensemble into an internal Raft log run by controller nodes: simpler ops, faster failover, more partitions. Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper mode.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.front: What does Strimzi do?
notes.back: A Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) operator: you declare Kafka, KafkaTopic, KafkaUser, KafkaConnect resources and it reconciles brokers as pods with persistent volume claims (PVCs), rolling restarts, TLS, and rebalancing.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.front: Why set broker.rack when Kafka spans availability zones (AZs)?
notes.back: So each partition's replicas are placed in different zones and replication factor (RF)=3 actually survives an AZ outage. It also enables fetch-from-follower.
notes.extra: Strimzi: rack.topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone + topologySpreadConstraints.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.front: When should you use Kafka Connect instead of writing a consumer?
notes.back: For plumbing: reusable source/sink connectors (Java Database Connectivity (JDBC), S3/Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS), Elasticsearch, Debezium) with offset tracking, task scaling and simple transforms. Write custom code only for business logic.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.front: How does Debezium capture changes from an online transaction processing (OLTP) database?
notes.back: As Kafka Connect source connectors reading the DB's own log (PostgreSQL replication slot, MySQL binlog, MongoDB oplog), emitting before/after row images. Captures deletes; no polling.
notes.extra: Managed alternatives: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) → Kinesis/Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK); Fabric mirroring.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.front: What's the main operational risk when a Debezium/change data capture (CDC) consumer stalls on PostgreSQL?
notes.back: The replication slot retains write-ahead log (WAL) until consumed, so the source's disk fills up.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.front: Why run a Schema Registry with Kafka?
notes.back: Messages carry a small schema ID instead of the schema, and the registry rejects incompatible schema versions before they break consumers.
notes.extra: Confluent, Apicurio, AWS Glue Schema Registry, Azure Schema Registry.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.text: Schema Registry modes: {{c1::BACKWARD}} (new schema reads old data) → upgrade {{c2::consumers}} first; {{c3::FORWARD}} (old schema reads new data) → upgrade {{c4::producers}} first; FULL = both.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.front: What is Kafka tiered storage (Kafka Improvement Proposal (KIP)-405)?
notes.back: Brokers keep recent segments on local disk and offload older ones to object storage, serving historical reads from there.
notes.extra: Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK) Provisioned, Confluent, Kafka ≥ 3.6 with a remote storage plugin.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.front: What does Kafka tiered storage change operationally?
notes.back: Retention is limited by cheap object storage, not broker disks; smaller disks mean faster re-replication and rebalancing; Kafka becomes a viable long-term replay store.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.front: When is Kafka Streams the right stream processor?
notes.back: Kafka-to-Kafka logic in a plain app: a Java library inside your Deployment, local RocksDB state backed by changelog topics, scale by pods ≤ partitions. Operationally light.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.front: When do you pick Apache Flink over Kafka Streams?
notes.back: Non-Kafka sources/sinks, very large state, complex event-time processing or SQL. It's a separate cluster (Flink K8s Operator; Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink).

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.front: What is a dead-letter topic, and why use one?
notes.back: A topic for records that still fail after retries, with error headers. Otherwise one poison record blocks every later record in its partition.
notes.analogy: A post office's undeliverable-mail bin: the problem letter is set aside so the rest of the mail keeps moving.
notes.extra: Alert on DLT growth and keep a replay tool.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.front: Managed open-source Kafka vs a provider-proprietary streaming service: trade-off?
notes.back:
Managed Kafka: real Kafka protocol and ecosystem (clients, Connect, Streams), long retention, portable.
Proprietary stream: capacity in provider units (shards), tight integration with the provider's serverless and delivery services; simpler but lock-in.
notes.extra: Example: Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK) vs Kinesis Data Streams (shards of 1 MB/s in, 2 MB/s out).

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.front: Kafka-protocol-compatible services that aren't Kafka: what works, and what doesn't?
notes.back: Kafka clients connect with a connection-string change, but the broker isn't Kafka: Connect, Streams and broker-side features (transactions, compaction details, tiered storage) may be missing or partial. Check feature parity before committing.
notes.extra: Examples: Azure Event Hubs (namespace ≈ cluster, event hub ≈ topic; partitions and consumer groups keep their names), Pub/Sub Kafka API, Redpanda, WarpStream.

notes.deck: Data Engineering::04 Kafka Ecosystem & Managed Streaming
notes.front: What is the 'stream capture to lake' pattern?
notes.back: The streaming platform automatically lands the raw stream as files (Avro/Parquet) in object storage, giving analytics a replayable raw layer without writing a consumer.
notes.extra: Examples: Event Hubs Capture → Blob/Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) Gen2; Kinesis Data Firehose → S3; Kafka Connect S3/Google Cloud Storage (GCS) sink.

notes.text: Capacity sizing: online transaction processing (OLTP) systems are sized by {{c1::transactions per second and p99 latency}}; online analytical processing (OLAP) systems by {{c2::scan throughput and concurrent queries}}.

notes.front: Why run analytics on a separate system from the online transaction processing (OLTP) database?
notes.back: Big scans evict the OLTP hot working set, hold long multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) snapshots (bloat) and contend with writers. And the layouts are opposite: rows + indexes vs columns + scans.

notes.front: How does data get from online transaction processing (OLTP) systems to analytics?
notes.back: Extract, transform, load (ETL)/extract, load, transform (ELT) batches, change data capture (CDC) streams (Debezium → Kafka → lake), or managed zero-ETL links (Aurora → Redshift zero-ETL; Azure SQL/Cosmos DB → Fabric mirroring).

notes.front: What is HTAP, and what do cloud vendors actually ship?
notes.back: One system for both workloads. In practice: two engines with managed replication into a columnar copy (Synapse Link, Fabric mirroring, AlloyDB columnar). Freshness is seconds to minutes.

notes.front: Star schema: fact vs dimension tables?
notes.back: Fact: one row per event (order line, reading), numeric measures + foreign keys; huge, append-mostly. Dimension: descriptive context (customer, product, date); small and wide.
notes.analogy: Receipts (facts) referencing a product catalogue and customer list (dimensions).
notes.extra: Small dimensions are copied to every node (Redshift DISTSTYLE ALL, Synapse REPLICATE).

notes.front: What is a Slowly Changing Dimension Type 2?
notes.back: Keeping history in a dimension by adding a new versioned row (with validity dates) when an attribute changes, instead of overwriting it.

notes.front: MPP warehouse architecture: what do the leader (coordinator) node and the compute nodes do?
notes.back: The leader parses, plans and coordinates; compute nodes hold slices of the data that scan in parallel (massively parallel processing).
notes.extra: Examples: Amazon Redshift, Synapse dedicated SQL pool (control node + 60 distributions), Greenplum.

notes.front: In a massively parallel processing (MPP) warehouse, what do distribution keys and sort/cluster keys control?
notes.back: Distribution key: which node a row lives on; co-locate join keys to avoid shuffles. Sort/cluster key: physical order, so min/max zone maps skip blocks.
notes.extra: Names: Redshift DISTKEY / SORTKEY; Synapse HASH distribution + clustered columnstore order; BigQuery clustering.

notes.text: Massively parallel processing (MPP) table distribution strategies: {{c1::hash on a column}} for large fact tables (high-cardinality join key); {{c2::round-robin}} (fastest load, joins shuffle); {{c3::replicate}} for small dimensions.
notes.extra: Names: Synapse HASH / ROUND_ROBIN / REPLICATE; Redshift DISTSTYLE KEY / EVEN / ALL.

notes.front: What pattern do Athena, Redshift Spectrum and Synapse serverless SQL share?
notes.back: Query in place over files in object storage via a metadata catalog (Glue, Fabric), billed per byte scanned.

notes.front: How do you make per-byte-scanned queries (Athena, serverless SQL) cheap?
notes.back: Columnar formats + compression, partitioning by prefix (e.g. dt=2026-09-13/) for directory pruning, and table formats for statistics.

notes.front: What is the small-files problem in a data lake?
notes.back: Millions of tiny files make per-file open/list/request overhead dominate scans and costs. Aim for ~128 MB–1 GB files; compact regularly.

notes.front: ETL vs ELT?
notes.back: Extract, transform, load (ETL): transform on a separate engine, then load the result. Extract, load, transform (ELT): load raw data into the warehouse/lake first, then transform there with SQL (dbt, Spark).
notes.analogy: ETL cooks at a central kitchen and delivers meals; ELT delivers the groceries and cooks in your kitchen.

notes.front: Why did the cloud push the industry toward extract, load, transform (ELT)?
notes.back: Cloud warehouses put cheap, elastic compute next to the data, so moving raw data once and transforming in place beats routing it through an external tool.

notes.front: What does 'separation of storage and compute' give a data platform?
notes.back: Data in shared object storage; stateless compute attaches on demand: independent scaling, pay-per-use, several engines on the same data, zero-copy sharing.
notes.analogy: A shared library with many reading rooms: add readers or rooms without copying the books.
notes.extra: Examples: Redshift RA3, Snowflake, Databricks, Trino on Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS)/Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS).

notes.front: What's the main trade-off of separating storage and compute?
notes.back: The network becomes the bottleneck, so engines rely on local SSD caches and compute must sit in the same region (ideally availability zone (AZ)) as the data.

notes.front: What is data gravity, and its design corollary?
notes.back: Large datasets pull applications toward them, because moving data is slow and costly (bandwidth, egress, consistency) while moving compute is cheap. Corollary: bring compute to the data.
notes.analogy: Like a big planet pulling moons into orbit: the bigger the dataset, the more systems end up circling it.

notes.text: Cloud network pricing (rough): same-availability-zone (AZ) private traffic is free; {{c1::cross-AZ}} costs ~$0.01/GB in each direction; cross-region ~$0.02/GB; {{c2::internet egress}} ~$0.05–0.09/GB.
notes.extra: Verify current regional pricing.

notes.front: Why can a chatty multi-availability-zone (AZ) microservice mesh or Kafka cluster surprise you on the bill?
notes.back: Every cross-AZ hop is billed per GB (on both sides on AWS), so replication and chatty calls can quietly cost more than the compute.

notes.front: What are the main costs of a multi-availability-zone (AZ) Kafka cluster, and the levers?
notes.back: Cross-AZ replication (compress, batch with linger.ms), cross-AZ consumer reads (fetch-from-follower), broker block storage (size by throughput; tiered storage).

notes.front: What is Kafka fetch-from-follower (Kafka Improvement Proposal (KIP)-392), and its trade-off?
notes.back: Consumers set client.rack and read from a replica in their own zone instead of the leader, cutting cross-availability-zone (AZ) traffic. Follower reads lag slightly behind the leader.

notes.front: Which Kubernetes features keep Service traffic inside one availability zone (AZ)?
notes.back: Even pod spread (topologySpreadConstraints on zone) plus trafficDistribution: PreferClose on the Service; meshes add locality load balancing (Istio).

notes.front: What's the risk of keeping traffic strictly zonal?
notes.back: Each zone must handle its own load, so a zone loss removes a third of capacity at once and unbalanced zones overload.

notes.front: Rule: where must state live if it has to survive a zone outage?
notes.back: On a regional service (S3, Blob zone-redundant storage (ZRS), Aurora, DynamoDB, Cosmos DB) or replicated by the application (Kafka in-sync replica set (ISR), DB replicas), never on a single zonal disk.

notes.text: {{c1::Zonal}} storage (one availability zone (AZ)): Elastic Block Store (EBS), instance store, single-AZ Relational Database Service (RDS), Azure locally redundant storage (LRS) Managed Disks. {{c2::Regional}} storage: S3, Elastic File System (EFS), Aurora storage, DynamoDB, Blob/Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) zone-redundant storage (ZRS), ZRS disks, Cosmos DB.

notes.front: Gateway/service endpoints vs PrivateLink/Private Endpoints for reaching S3/Blob?
notes.back: S3 Gateway Endpoint / Azure Service Endpoint: free, route-based, stays on the backbone. PrivateLink / Private Endpoint: a private IP in your virtual network (VNet)/virtual private cloud (VPC); hourly + per-GB fee.

notes.front: Why route Kubernetes-to-object-storage traffic through private endpoints?
notes.back: It avoids network address translation (NAT) gateway per-GB fees (~$0.045/GB on AWS) and lets bucket policies deny all public access.

notes.front: Why do hybrid platforms often keep compute on-premises?
notes.back: Master data (enterprise resource planning (ERP), sensor archives, regulated records) lives there; its gravity, residency rules and link bandwidth pull processing to it.

notes.front: How much data can a 1 Gbps Direct Connect / ExpressRoute link move per day?
notes.back: About 10 TB/day. Provisioned bandwidth is a hard cap on migration speed.

notes.text: Running cloud services on-prem: AWS offers {{c1::Outposts}} and Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) Anywhere; Azure offers {{c2::Azure Arc}} (Arc-enabled Kubernetes and data services) and Azure Local.

notes.front: What's the trap with cold/archive storage tiers?
notes.back: Retrieval fees, minimum storage periods (30/90/180 days) and hours of rehydration latency. Archiving data you'll replay or audit is a false economy.
notes.extra: Millions of small objects make per-request and transition fees dominate.

notes.text: Storage tiers: S3 goes Standard → Intelligent-Tiering → {{c1::Standard-IA}} → Glacier Instant/Flexible → {{c2::Glacier Deep Archive}}; Azure Blob goes Hot → Cool → Cold → {{c3::Archive}}.
notes.extra: IA: infrequent access.

notes.front: Which platform controls enforce data residency?
notes.back: Region allow-lists (AWS service control policies (SCPs), Azure Policy allowedLocations), in-jurisdiction replication, region-bound customer-managed keys, and admission policies placing workloads only in allowed regions.

notes.front: Placing a new stream-processing service: what's the first question?
notes.back: Where is the largest input dataset (Kafka cluster, lake bucket)? Put compute in that region and availability zone (AZ) set.

notes.front: Where should a data service write its output?
notes.back: Next to its consumers: the lake for analytics, an online transaction processing (OLTP) store for serving. Justify every cross-region or internet flow.

notes.front: If a new dataset may become the next centre of gravity, what should you choose up front?
notes.back: Open formats (Parquet, Iceberg, Delta), so future engines and clouds can use the data without migration lock-in.
